question: Extend the year-by-year sector mix back to FY2019-FY2020 (the DAFRC panel and netpayout990 cache start FY2019/2020) with the same script, to test whether the FY2021 human-services peak (17.7% of DAF-weighted dollars, all itemising sponsors) is a pandemic-era level rather than a baseline
conclusion_affected: Reading of the FY2021-24 human services decline (-2.4 pts) as normalisation vs secular shift
rationale: FY2021 is the first year covered; human services falls from 17.7% to 13.9% (FY2023) and recovers to 15.2% (FY2024), so the start year may be a high point. Two earlier years would separate the two readings

question: SVCF FY2022 non-itemised line 1: explain the $1.57bn gap between Part IX line 1 ($3.63bn) and Schedule I ($2.06bn) on SVCF's FY2022 return (itemises 57%, so it is treated as a full itemiser and the gap is allocated as sub-$5,000 grants). Read the return's Schedule I supplemental text and SVCF's audited FY2022 statements
conclusion_affected: The FY2022 full-layer sector shares (the sub-$5k layer adds $2.31bn at the top 50 in FY2022 against $0.67-1.25bn in other years)
rationale: The b40n120201-01 50% rule was written for FY2023-24; in FY2022 one sponsor-year supplies most of the sub-$5k component, so FY2022 full-layer shares carry an allocation artefact. The sched_i layer avoids it

question: Religion's rising share (+2.5 pts FY2021-24, broad-based: top-10 recipients explain +0.3 pts): split NTEE X dollars by congregation vs religious-affiliated nonprofit (BMF FOUNDATION 10 vs X with NTEE subcodes) and by sponsor segment, and test against Giving USA's religion series
conclusion_affected: Whether DAF money is shifting toward congregations or toward faith-based service charities
rationale: The shift survives fixed panels, SVCF/CZ exclusion, both bases and both layers, and no single recipient drives it. Its composition is unknown

question: Recipient-side BMF survivorship: re-classify FY2021-22 recipients missing from the November 2026 BMF using an archived 2022 BMF snapshot (IRS EO BMF archive or the IRS revocation list), and measure how much of the FY2021 unclassified share (6.4%) is recipients that lost status after 2022
conclusion_affected: The unclassified-share decline (-0.8 pts) and small-sector trends
rationale: One 2026 BMF snapshot is applied to all four years; EIN-not-in-BMF dollars are 2.2% in FY2021 against 1.9% in FY2024, so survivorship bias exists but is small

question: Johns Hopkins University receipts from DAF sponsors (DAF-weighted $192m FY2021, $272m FY2022, $1.56bn FY2023, $1.04bn FY2024): identify the granting sponsors and whether a single donor pledge drives them, and report education's trend with and without it
conclusion_affected: Education's share trend (-0.9 pts FY2021-24; about -2.7 pts on the itemised layer ex JHU)
rationale: One recipient adds +1.4 pts to education over FY2021-24 and +2.7 pts FY2022-23, larger than the sector's net change; the underlying education trend is therefore more negative than the headline

question: Annual refresh rule: when FY2025 returns are in the netpayout990 cache, rerun scripts/mission_sector_mix_trend.py with FYS extended, and report each sector's change against the FY2021-24 envelope of the robustness variants (changing/fixed panel, ex SVCF, ex CZ, both bases, both layers)
conclusion_affected: Ongoing sector-trend claims in FINAL-STATUS / industry report
rationale: Year-on-year moves of 2-3 pts are produced by single grants (CZ LLCs $1.66bn, Further Future Foundation $1.31bn, JHU), so a trend claim needs the variant envelope, not one series
